strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in LLM inference scaling with the first rigorous analytical framework
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with multiple complementary perspectives (deterministic equivalents, high-T expansion, extreme value theory)
Novel insights including optimal reward differing from teacher, existence of optimal k under misspecification, and optimal temperature for reward selection
Strong experimental validation on toy model with perfect theory-experiment agreement (Figure 2)
Empirical validation on real LLMs reveals new phenomena (optimal T) supporting theoretical predictions
Mathematically sound with rigorous proofs and correct application of advanced techniques (deterministic equivalents, extreme value theory)
Clear presentation with well-organized progression from theory to experiments
weaknesses: Significant gap between theoretical model (linear, quadratic reward, Gaussian inputs) and practical LLMs (nonlinear, learned rewards, discrete tokens)
Incomplete quantitative validation on LLMs - Figure 12 notes exponent of k differs from theoretical k^(-2) prediction, indicating theory may not fully capture LLM behavior
Limited practical applicability - formulas for optimal T and reward require unknown quantities (m(x), s(x), BR) with no guidance for estimation
Results mostly confirm empirically known phenomena rather than providing surprising new insights
Restrictive and hard-to-verify assumptions: Result 1 requires σ ≪ σ_c(α,R) with poorly characterized threshold; independence assumption violated in practice
High variance in some LLM experiments (Figs 8-9) and evaluation limited to single task (GSM8K) and domain (math)
Trade-off analysis (Remark 6) applies only to specific parameter regimes with limited real-world relevance
Inconsistency between theoretical generalization error (squared error, Eq. 8) and LLM metric (accuracy, Eq. 27) makes direct mapping unclear
